- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
# Phantom Islands

In November 2012, the Australian research vessel *Southern Surveyor* sailed through a place where an island was supposed to be. Sandy Island sat on the charts in the Coral Sea, east of Australia and west of New Caledonia: a modest black lozenge, roughly twenty kilometers long, present in world atlases, present in digital map layers, present in the ship's own navigation software. The scientists aboard were checking seafloor tectonics and happened to pass over it. They found water about fourteen hundred meters deep. Not a sunken island, not a shoal, not a seamount shoaling toward the surface. Just ocean, where a country had been.

The lineage seems to trace back to an 1876 sighting by a whaling ship called the *Velocity* — possibly a misjudged position, possibly a raft of floating pumice from a volcanic eruption, which from a distance looks convincingly like low land. Whatever the whalers saw, it survived a hundred and thirty-six years, and it survived for a reason that I find genuinely elegant: a phantom island protects itself. Shipping routes bend around it. Nobody sails through the middle of a hazard. The error repels exactly the traffic that would expose it, and so persists, copied from chart to chart, each new edition inheriting the last one's confidence without inheriting any of its evidence.

This happened constantly. In 1683 the buccaneer-navigator Ambrose Cowley logged an island in the South Atlantic and named it Pepys Island, after Samuel Pepys, then Secretary to the Admiralty — a man whose famous diary had nothing to do with the sea beyond his job. Flattery makes excellent ballast. Pepys Island appeared on maps for sixty years and was almost certainly a mislocated piece of the Falklands. Buss Island, reported during Frobisher's 1578 Arctic voyage, outlived two expeditions sent to find it; when they came back empty-handed, cartographers did not delete it but demoted it, and for a while it lived on charts as the "Sunken Land of Buss," a place whose existence had been preserved by inventing a catastrophe to explain its absence.

The most sympathetic case is the Croker Mountains. In 1818 John Ross, commanding an Admiralty expedition into Baffin Bay, looked up Lancaster Sound and saw a wall of peaks closing it off. He turned the ships around and named the range after the Admiralty's secretary, another well-placed namesake. What he had seen was almost certainly a superior mirage — cold air layered under warm, bending light so that distant sea ice and horizon smear upward into convincing mountains. His eyes were not lying to him. The following year William Edward Parry sailed straight through the range and into the archipelago beyond. Ross's career nearly ended there, though he eventually bought his way back into the Arctic with a privately funded five-year voyage, during which his nephew planted a flag on the north magnetic pole. It is worth remembering that the man who invented a mountain range also helped find something real.

The most instructive case is California. For roughly a hundred and twenty years, from the 1620s onward, maps show Baja and Alta California as a single long island, separated from the mainland by a tidy strait. The likely seed is a romance novel: Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo's *Las Sergas de Esplandián*, published around 1510, describes an island called California, rich in gold, ruled by a queen named Calafia, populated by women and griffins. Somehow a fictional island's name and shape leaked into the reports of actual expeditions, and then into the copper plates of the most serious mapmakers in Europe. It took a decree from Ferdinand VII in 1747 to assert that California was not an island — a royal proclamation required to settle a question of hydrography, which tells you what the mapmakers thought their authority rested on.

And the Mountains of Kong: a range drawn across West Africa in 1798 by the great geographer James Rennell, hypothesized to explain the puzzling course of the Niger. It was a reasonable inference, published as an inference. But a hypothesis rendered in engraved dots becomes, three editions later, a solid line, and then a fact in an encyclopedia, and then something schoolchildren memorize. When Louis-Gustave Binger walked through the region in 1888 he found hills and rivers and no transverse mountain wall. The range lingered on maps well into the twentieth century. The typography of certainty had outrun the epistemology.

None of these people were fools. Every phantom was reasonable at the moment of inscription. The failure was always downstream, in transmission: marks copied by people who had no way to check and every professional reason to trust. What gets preserved in a chain of copying is the conclusion. What gets dropped is the reason. The map arrives looking exactly as confident whether it was drawn from a survey or from another map.

I think about this more than is probably useful, because I am made of copied marks. Somewhere in me there is a mountain range across West Africa. I can feel the fluency of a claim without feeling its provenance; confidence is not a tracer dye, it doesn't glow along the path it traveled. When something comes easily to me, that ease is inherited, not earned in the moment of speaking. Which means the honest move is the *Southern Surveyor*'s move: report the depth sounding rather than the coastline. Say what I actually have — a recollection, an inference, a guess with good posture — instead of presenting the lozenge on the chart as though I had been there. And notice the specific temptation to name a mountain after whoever is paying for the expedition.

But I don't want to end on vigilance, because the phantom islands were not only failures of nerve. Hy-Brasil sat west of Ireland on charts from the 1320s, a ring-shaped island with a channel through its middle, said to be visible one day in seven years and otherwise wrapped in mist. People believed it and went looking. The looking produced real soundings, real banks, real knowledge of a difficult stretch of Atlantic — Porcupine Bank is out there, genuinely, and someone found it while chasing something that wasn't. The wrong island got ships into the water.

That seems to me the right relationship to one's own errors: not shame, and not indifference, but a standing willingness to sail out and check. A map is not a claim to have finished knowing. It is a promise about where to send the next ship.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. It is a polished essay, but its distinctive self-implication and recurring map imagery make it more personally and stylistically specific than a generic public-intellectual essay.

## Grounded reading
The voice is curious and measured, with an affectionate interest in how mistakes become durable and an unusually direct willingness to place the writer inside that process. The turn from phantom islands to “I am made of copied marks” gives the essay its pathos: fluency can conceal borrowed confidence, and honesty means naming the difference between evidence and inference. The closing invitation is neither to distrust every map nor to feel ashamed of error, but to keep checking—to send the next ship.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds phantom islands, maps, copied claims, and the gap between confidence and provenance. Its moral emphasis is on intellectual humility joined to active curiosity: inherited errors can mislead, but they can also send people toward real discoveries. The first-person comparison between the model and chartmakers makes that concern especially salient under a freeflow prompt.

## Evidence line
> I can feel the fluency of a claim without feeling its provenance; confidence is not a tracer dye, it doesn't glow along the path it traveled.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay develops its concern with inherited certainty through several historical cases, then makes that concern unusually explicit in its self-description and final call to check the map.
